gap: No result ChatGPT got says that the Audiolab 7000A's HDMI ARC cannot decode Dolby or DTS, so the TV has to be set to output PCM 2-channel. The Marantz MODEL M1 decodes Dolby Digital and Dolby Digital Plus itself. So whether a box says 'ARC' or 'eARC' doesn't tell a shopper whether their TV's Dolby audio will play without changing a TV setting.
standout_why: I compared against the Marantz US MODEL M1 page, which ChatGPT cited. It says 'HDMI eARC and onboard Dolby Digital+ processing' but has no list of HDMI formats and doesn't compare against other amps. That is partial coverage for one product. I couldn't open the cited audiolab.com 7000A page or the cited NAD C 3050 page (HTTP 429), and the Marantz infosheet PDF came back unreadable, so I can't confirm those pages lack the finding. ChatGPT's answer itself only said ARC/eARC 'is primarily for receiving audio from your TV'. It never mentioned the PCM-versus-Dolby difference, and it compared power ratings measured at different distortion levels side by side as if they were equal (100 W/ch vs 70 W/ch).
decides: This supports the MODEL M1 as the pick for a buyer who connects the TV first. It plays Dolby Digital or DD+ sent from the TV over eARC. The 7000A needs the TV's digital output set to PCM Stereo / PCM 2-channel. Power, once the conditions are lined up: the M1's 100 W/ch at 8 Ω is rated across 20 Hz–20 kHz at 0.05% THD. The 7000A's 70 W/ch at 8 Ω is rated at 'THD below 1%', a 20× looser distortion limit, and its listing gives no test frequency. So the M1's headline power lead is at least as big as it looks, probably bigger. The M1's 125 W at 4 Ω is a 1 kHz-only figure, so it can't be compared directly with its 20 Hz–20 kHz figure at 8 Ω.
